questions.q: In the current Salesforce model, what is the difference between an External Credential and a Named Credential?
options: They are two names for exactly the same thing
The Named Credential holds the secret; the External Credential holds only the URL
External Credentials are used only in Flow, Named Credentials only in Apex
The External Credential holds authentication parameters and secret-storage configuration; the Named Credential holds the callout endpoint URL and references the External Credential
questions.explain: The current two-piece model separates authentication (External Credential) from the endpoint URL (Named Credential, which references the External Credential) -- the older single-definition style is deprecated.

questions.q: Why does the ApplianceMakers Warranty integration use a Named Principal rather than a Per-User principal?
options: Named Principal is required for all outbound callouts
The manufacturer's API doesn't need to know which individual Solstice employee submitted a claim, only that Solstice submitted it -- one shared identity is appropriate
Per-User principals are not supported in Apex callouts
Named Principal is faster than Per-User in every case
questions.explain: Named Principal uses one shared identity for all users making the callout, which fits since the external system only needs to know Solstice submitted the claim, not which employee.

questions.q: What distinguishes `ManufacturerWarrantyTransientException` from `ManufacturerWarrantyRejectedException` in this lesson's design?
options: A transient exception represents a failure worth retrying (e.g. a timeout); a rejected exception represents a failure that will recur identically on retry and needs human attention instead
They are functionally identical, just named differently for readability
Rejected exceptions are always retried; transient exceptions are never retried
Transient exceptions can only be thrown from Batch Apex
questions.explain: The two subtypes let the Queueable react differently: retry for a transient failure like a timeout, but flag for manual review on a rejected failure like an invalid serial number that won't succeed on retry.

questions.q: Why does the Queueable's retry logic use a capped `attemptsRemaining` counter instead of retrying indefinitely?
options: Apex does not allow any loops in Queueable classes
Retrying more than once is against Salesforce's terms of service
An indefinitely retried job against a prolonged outage would keep re-enqueuing and could eventually run into the shared 24-hour asynchronous Apex limit
attemptsRemaining is required syntax with no functional effect
questions.explain: A capped retry count prevents an extended external outage from causing indefinite re-enqueuing, which would also risk exhausting the org's shared async Apex limit.

questions.q: Why does catching `ManufacturerWarrantyRejectedException` and `ManufacturerWarrantyTransientException` separately matter, instead of one broad `catch (Exception e)`?
options: Separate catches run faster than one broad catch
It lets the handler make a genuinely different decision -- give up and flag for a human vs. retry -- based on which specific failure occurred
Apex does not allow catching a general Exception type
It has no real benefit; it's purely a style preference
questions.explain: The whole point of the exception subtypes is that the calling code can react differently depending on the specific failure, which a single broad catch block couldn't distinguish.
